title: Internet Group Management Protocol, Version 3
summary: Specifies IGMPv3, the protocol IPv4 systems use to tell neighboring multicast routers which multicast groups they want to join. Version 3 adds source filtering, so a host can ask for traffic only from certain senders, or from everyone except certain senders. It updates RFC 2236 and was replaced by RFC 9776.

plainLanguage.summary:
Multicast is a way to send one message to many computers at once. Before the traffic can flow, each router has to know which machines nearby want it.

IGMP is how they find out. Version 3 lets a machine be picky: it can say it wants the traffic only from certain senders, or from everyone except certain senders.

subtitle: How IPv4 hosts tell routers which multicast groups they want, and which senders they want to hear from.

tldr.problem: Multicast routers need to know which groups the systems on each attached network want to receive, and earlier IGMP versions could not say which senders were wanted.
tldr.mechanism: Routers send periodic Queries and hosts answer with Version 3 Membership Reports that carry a group, a filter mode of INCLUDE or EXCLUDE, and a list of source addresses.
tldr.outcome: IGMPv3 adds source filtering while staying interoperable with Versions 1 and 2. The RFC was later obsoleted by RFC 9776.

today: RFC 3376 was a Proposed Standard and it obsoleted RFC 2236. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9776, which is the current version of the Internet Group Management Protocol, and was updated by RFC 4604.

sections.title: What IGMP Does
sections.content:
The Internet Group Management Protocol (IGMP) is used by IPv4 systems, hosts and routers, to report their IP multicast group memberships to any neighbouring multicast routers. A multicast router may itself be a member of one or more groups, in which case it performs both the multicast router part of the protocol, collecting the membership information its multicast routing protocol needs, and the group member part, telling itself and other neighbouring routers about its own memberships.

IGMP is also used for other IP multicast management functions, with message types other than those used for group membership reporting. This document specifies only the group membership reporting functions and messages.

Version 1, in RFC 1112, was the first widely deployed version and the first to become an Internet Standard. Version 2, in RFC 2236, added low leave latency, a reduction in the time a multicast router takes to learn that no members of a group remain on an attached network. Version 3 adds source filtering, the ability of a system to report interest in packets only from specific source addresses, as needed for Source-Specific Multicast, or from all but specific source addresses. That information may be used by multicast routing protocols to avoid delivering packets from specific sources to networks where nobody is listening. Version 3 is designed to interoperate with Versions 1 and 2.

Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) is used in a similar way by IPv6 systems. MLD version 1 implements the functionality of IGMP version 2, and MLD version 2 implements the functionality of IGMP version 3.
sections.plainLanguage:
When a video is streamed to many people, the routers between the sender and the viewers have to know who wants it, or they will carry traffic nobody is watching.

IGMP is how the viewers tell the nearest router.

sections.title: The Interface an Application Uses
sections.content:
Within an IP system there is, at least conceptually, a service interface that upper-layer protocols or application programs use to ask the IP layer to enable and disable reception of packets sent to specific multicast addresses. To take full advantage of IGMPv3, that interface must support one operation:

IPMulticastListen(socket, interface, multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list)

The socket parameter is an implementation-specific value that distinguishes between different requesting entities within the system, such as programs or processes; the socket parameter of BSD Unix system calls is a specific example.

The interface parameter is a local identifier of the network interface on which reception is to be enabled or disabled. Interfaces may be physical, such as an Ethernet interface, or virtual, such as the endpoint of a Frame Relay virtual circuit or of an IP-in-IP tunnel. An implementation may allow a special unspecified value, in which case the request applies to the primary or default interface. If reception of the same multicast address is wanted on more than one interface, the operation is invoked separately for each.

The multicast-address parameter is the group the request concerns, and the operation is invoked separately for each additional group on a given interface.

The filter-mode parameter is either INCLUDE or EXCLUDE. In INCLUDE mode, reception of packets sent to the multicast address is requested only from the source addresses in the source list. In EXCLUDE mode, reception is requested from all source addresses except those in the list.

The source-list parameter is an unordered list of zero or more IP unicast addresses. An implementation may impose a limit on the size of source lists, but that limit must not be less than 64 addresses per list, and when an operation would exceed the limit the interface must return an error.

For a given combination of socket, interface and multicast address, only a single filter mode and source list can be in effect at a time. Either the filter mode, or the source list, or both, may be changed by later requests with the same three values, and each later request completely replaces any earlier one.

Earlier versions of IGMP did not support source filters and had a simpler interface of Join and Leave operations, enabling and disabling reception from all sources. The Join operation is equivalent to IPMulticastListen(socket, interface, multicast-address, EXCLUDE, {}), and the Leave operation to IPMulticastListen(socket, interface, multicast-address, INCLUDE, {}), where the braces denote an empty source list.
sections.plainLanguage:
An application asks the IP layer for one thing: listen to this group, on this interface, from these senders only, or from anyone but these senders.

The empty list is the important special case. An empty INCLUDE list means stop listening, and an empty EXCLUDE list means listen to everybody.

sections.title: The State a System Keeps
sections.content:
For each socket on which the listen operation has been invoked, the system records the desired reception state for that socket. That state conceptually consists of a set of records of the form (interface, multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list). The state evolves with each invocation. If the requested filter mode is INCLUDE and the requested source list is empty, the entry for that interface and address is deleted if it is present, and if it is not present the request is ignored. If the requested filter mode is EXCLUDE, or the source list is non-empty, the entry for that interface and address is changed to the requested filter mode and source list, or a new entry is created if there was none.

Besides the per-socket state, a system must also maintain or compute reception state for each of its interfaces, conceptually a set of records of the form (multicast-address, filter-mode, source-list). At most one record exists per multicast address for a given interface. This per-interface state is derived from the per-socket state, but may differ from it when different sockets have differing filter modes or source lists for the same address and interface. If one socket asks for sources a, b and c and another asks for b, c and d, the interface must receive packets from any of a, b, c or d to satisfy both, so the interface record is INCLUDE with the list {a, b, c, d}.

After a multicast packet has been accepted from an interface by the IP layer, its delivery to a particular socket depends on that socket's own reception state, and possibly on other conditions such as the transport-layer port the socket is bound to. In the example, a packet from source a would be delivered on the first socket but not on the second. IGMP Queries and Reports are not subject to source filtering and must always be processed by hosts and routers.

The rules for deriving the interface state are as follows. For each distinct interface and multicast address pair appearing in any socket state, a per-interface record is created. Considering all socket records with that pair: if any such record has a filter mode of EXCLUDE, the interface record is EXCLUDE, and its source list is the intersection of the source lists of all the socket records in EXCLUDE mode, minus those source addresses that appear in any socket record in INCLUDE mode. If all the records are INCLUDE, the interface record is INCLUDE and its source list is the union of the source lists of all the socket records. An implementation must not use an EXCLUDE interface record to represent a group when all sockets for that group are in INCLUDE state, and if system resource limits are reached while an interface state source list is calculated, an error must be returned to the application that requested the operation. These rules are re-evaluated whenever a listen invocation modifies the socket state, and a change of socket state does not necessarily change the interface state.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two programs on the same machine can each ask for a different set of senders. The machine works out the union of what they need, because that is the only way to satisfy both.

When the sets disagree about include or exclude, the machine has to be careful: it must not deliver more than the applications asked for.

sections.title: The Messages
sections.content:
IGMP messages are encapsulated in IPv4 datagrams with an IP protocol number of 2. Every IGMP message in this document is sent with an IP Time-to-Live of 1, IP Precedence of Internetwork Control, for example Type of Service 0xc0, and carries an IP Router Alert option in its IP header.

Two message types concern the IGMPv3 protocol: type 0x11, the Membership Query, and type 0x22, the Version 3 Membership Report. An implementation of IGMPv3 must also support three message types for interoperation with earlier versions: 0x12, the Version 1 Membership Report, 0x16, the Version 2 Membership Report, and 0x17, the Version 2 Leave Group. Unrecognised message types must be silently ignored.

Membership Queries are sent by multicast routers to query the reception state of neighbouring interfaces. The message holds a type field, a Max Resp Code, a checksum, a group address, a reserved field, the S flag, the querier's robustness variable, the querier's query interval code and the number of source addresses, followed by the source addresses themselves. The Max Resp Code field gives the maximum time allowed before sending a responding report; the actual time is in units of a tenth of a second, and small values let a router tune the leave latency, the time between the last host leaving a group and the routing protocol being told there are no more members. The group address is zero for a General Query and the address being queried for a Group-Specific or Group-and-Source-Specific Query. The S flag, when set, tells receiving routers to suppress the normal timer updates they would perform on hearing a query, though it does not suppress the querier election or the host-side processing a router may have to do as a group member. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the whole IGMP message, and it must be verified before a packet is processed.

Version 3 Membership Reports carry a number of group records, each holding a record type, an auxiliary data length, the number of source addresses, the multicast address, the source addresses and any auxiliary data. IGMPv3 defines no auxiliary data, so implementations must not include any when transmitting and must ignore any they receive. If the IP header's packet length indicates additional octets beyond the last group record, those octets must be included in the checksum computation but otherwise ignored.

There are six group record types. A Current-State Record is sent in response to a query and reports the current reception state of the interface for a single multicast address; its type is either 1, MODE_IS_INCLUDE, or 2, MODE_IS_EXCLUDE. A Filter-Mode-Change Record is sent when the interface-level filter mode for an address changes, and its type is either 3, CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE, or 4, CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE. A Source-List-Change Record is sent when the source list changes without a change of filter mode, and its type is either 5, ALLOW_NEW_SOURCES, or 6, BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES. If a change results in both allowing new sources and blocking old ones, two group records are sent for the same multicast address. Unrecognised record types must be silently ignored.

Reports are sent with a valid IP source address for the destination subnet. The address 0.0.0.0 may be used by a system that has not yet acquired an IP address, and routers must accept a report with that source address.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two kinds of message do the work. A router asks, with a Query. A host answers, with a Report that lists the groups it cares about and the senders it wants or does not want.

The Report can also say that something just changed, rather than restating everything.

sections.title: How Hosts, Routers and Timers Fit Together
sections.content:
The protocol has two halves. The group member part covers what a host does: it responds to queries with reports describing its current state, and it sends reports of its own when the local state changes. The multicast router part covers what a router does: it sends periodic general queries, it keeps the state of each group on each interface, and it decides when a group has no members left and tells the multicast routing protocol.

Several timers drive the exchange, and most of them are configurable. If non-default settings are used they must be consistent among all systems on a single link. The Robustness Variable allows tuning for expected packet loss, because IGMP is robust to that many packet losses; it must not be zero and should not be one, and the default is 2. The Query Interval, the interval between general queries sent by the querier, defaults to 125 seconds; larger values mean fewer IGMP messages on the network. The Query Response Interval is the Max Response Time used in the periodic general queries, with a default of 100, which is 10 seconds; larger values make the traffic less bursty by spreading host responses out, and the number of seconds it represents must be less than the Query Interval. The Group Membership Interval is the time that must pass before a router decides there are no more members of a group or source on a network, and it must be the Robustness Variable times the Query Interval plus one Query Response Interval. The Other Querier Present Interval must be the Robustness Variable times the Query Interval plus half of one Query Response Interval. The Startup Query Interval is the interval between general queries on startup, by default a quarter of the Query Interval, and the Startup Query Count is the number of queries sent on startup, by default the Robustness Variable. The Last Member Query Interval is the Max Response Time used in the group-specific queries sent in response to leave messages, with a default of 10, which is 1 second, and it tunes the leave latency of the network. The Last Member Query Count is the number of group-specific queries sent before the router assumes there are no local members, by default the Robustness Variable.

Because a router may be asked to leave a group, and other routers need to hear about it, Version 3 has to interoperate with the earlier versions. A router keeps track of which version of members it has heard from, because a Version 1 membership report tells the router that members exist but says nothing about which sources they want, so the router cannot use source-specific information for that group while it is in that state. A router can be configured to ignore Version 1 messages entirely, which restores full behaviour at the cost of automatic compatibility with Version 1 hosts, and the same choice exists for Version 2 messages.
sections.plainLanguage:
Everything runs on timers. A router asks regularly, a host answers within a deadline, and a router waits a while before deciding that nobody is listening any more.

The timers are deliberately generous, because a lost report should not look like an empty group.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC considers what a forged message of each type would do, and describes the use of IPsec Authentication Header to authenticate messages if desired.

A forged Query from a machine with a lower IP address than the current querier causes the querier duties to be assigned to the forger. If the forger then sends no more queries, the Other Querier Present timer times out and another router takes over. In the meantime, if the forger ignores leave messages, traffic might flow to groups with no members for up to the Group Membership Interval. A denial-of-service attack on a host could be staged with forged group-and-source-specific queries: the attacker learns a host's membership with a general query, then sends many group-and-source-specific queries, each with a large source list and a large Maximum Response Time, so the host has to store and maintain all those sources until it sends its delayed response. To protect against this, a host stack implementation could restrict the number of group-and-source-specific queries per group membership within the interval, and record only a limited number of sources.

Three measures defend against externally forged queries. Routers should not forward queries, which is easier if the query carries the Router Alert option. Hosts should ignore version 2 or 3 queries without the Router Alert option. And hosts should ignore version 1, 2 or 3 general queries sent to a multicast address other than 224.0.0.1, the all-systems address.

A forged Report may make routers think there are members of a group when there are not. Forged reports from the local network are meaningless, since joining a group on a host is generally an unprivileged operation and a local user can achieve the same result without forging anything. For external sources there are two defences: ignore the report if the source address cannot be identified as belonging to a network assigned to the interface on which the packet arrived, though reports with a source address of 0.0.0.0 should be accepted on any interface; and ignore reports without Router Alert options and require that routers do not forward report messages, which breaks backwards compatibility with implementations of IGMPv1 or earlier versions of IGMPv2 that did not require Router Alert. A forged Version 1 report may put a router into a state where it ignores leave messages, so traffic can flow to groups with no members for up to the Group Membership Interval; a configuration switch to ignore Version 1 messages completely solves this, at the cost of automatic compatibility with Version 1 hosts, so it should be used only where fast leave is critical. A forged Version 2 report may put a router into a state where it ignores IGMPv3 source-specific state messages, so traffic can flow from unwanted sources for up to the Group Membership Interval, and the same switch exists.

A forged State-Change Report causes the querier to send group-specific or source-and-group-specific queries for that group, which causes extra processing on each router and each member of the group but cannot cause the loss of desired traffic. The defences are again to ignore reports whose source address cannot be tied to the receiving interface, and to ignore reports without Router Alert options.
sections.plainLanguage:
Anyone on the network can send a fake IGMP message, and the RFC goes through what each kind of forgery would achieve.

The defences are mostly about not believing reports from outside the network, and about ignoring anything that arrives without the option that marks it as a control message.

fields.name: Max Resp Code
fields.desc: Maximum time before a report, in units of a tenth of a second.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement of the one's complement sum of the message.

fields.name: Resv, S, QRV
fields.desc: Reserved bits, the suppress-router-side flag and the querier's robustness variable.

fields.name: QQIC
fields.desc: The querier's query interval code, in seconds.

items.label: MEMBERSHIP QUERY
items.desc: Sent by routers to ask neighbouring hosts what they are receiving.

items.label: VERSION 3 MEMBERSHIP REPORT
items.desc: Sent by hosts to report their state and their changes.

items.label: VERSION 1 MEMBERSHIP REPORT
items.desc: Supported for interoperability with older hosts.

items.label: VERSION 2 MEMBERSHIP REPORT
items.desc: Supported for interoperability with older hosts.

items.label: VERSION 2 LEAVE GROUP
items.desc: A host telling its router it is leaving a group.

items.title: 1 MODE_IS_INCLUDE
items.text: Answers a query with the current state of one group.

items.title: 2 MODE_IS_EXCLUDE
items.text: Answers a query with the current state of one group.

items.title: 3 CHANGE_TO_INCLUDE_MODE
items.text: Reports that the interface switched to INCLUDE for a group.

items.title: 4 CHANGE_TO_EXCLUDE_MODE
items.text: Reports that the interface switched to EXCLUDE for a group.

items.title: 5 ALLOW_NEW_SOURCES
items.text: Reports sources the system now wants to hear from.

items.title: 6 BLOCK_OLD_SOURCES
items.text: Reports sources the system no longer wants to hear from.
